topic: code understanding; code comments; documentation quality
status: bounded synthesis of two full-text empirical studies, one same-group follow-up and one task-aware code-completion study
claim: Current evidence does not support a general rule that more comments improve code understanding. A narrower and more defensible pattern is that comments can help when they convey relevant intent, while stale, unrelated or misleading comments can harm; the size and even presence of a benefit depends on task, model, and measurement proxy.
positive_evidence: The 2025 legacy-assembler study reports generally higher quiz scores as comments increase, and a 12-point drop on the advanced questions under wholly inaccurate comments (73% with accurate comments vs 61% with inaccurate comments).
Macke and Doyle's 2024 NAACL HumanEval unit-test study finds that random/wrong comments significantly harm generated-test success, and comments increase line coverage.
counterevidence: In the 2024 HumanEval study, ordinary correct comments did not significantly improve test success vs no comments; increased line coverage did not translate into significantly higher pass rate.
In the 2025 single-module study, 20% inaccurate comments had negligible effect for three of four models, and no-code quiz performance averaged 75%, suggesting possible memorization.
The 2024 study shares both authors with the 2025 arXiv paper, so the results are not an independent replication; both are narrow benchmark proxies, not real maintenance workflows.

sources.title: Testing the Effect of Code Documentation on Large Language Model Code Understanding
sources.sections: Secs. 3-7: HumanEval unit-test proxy, null correct-comment success effect, wrong-comment harm and limitations

falsifiable_test: Run a preregistered, multi-language and multi-backbone study on fresh, post-cutoff repositories with a 2x2 documentation design (absent vs accurate vs stale/wrong vs irrelevant), randomize MCQ answer positions, and measure both code-question accuracy and executed maintenance/test outcomes. A comment-volume benefit claim weakens if accurate comments do not improve held-out performance over no comments; a reliability-specific claim weakens if wrong/stale comments do not raise errors or contradiction rates. Track contamination and document source provenance.
limitations: Two sampled primary studies and a same-group follow-up; one is a single assembler module with MCQA and the other uses HumanEval unit-test generation. No broad multi-language external replication or developer maintenance study was run. Do not claim prevalence or novelty.

topic: code LLM instruction tuning; fill-in-the-middle completion; model capabilities
status: bounded synthesis of one sampled multi-family study and one full-text task-specific follow-up
claim: Generic instruction tuning often shifts code models toward instruction-conditioned generation and away from FIM infilling in the tested benchmarks, but the tradeoff is not inevitable: an objective that structurally separates instructions inside FIM can recover instruction following while usually preserving no-instruction infilling. The evidence remains local-context and two-family, not a general guarantee.
positive_evidence: The sampled Code Talkers study compares Qwen2.5-Coder (1.5B-32B) and DeepSeek-Coder (1.3B-33B) and reports frequent FIM regressions alongside gains on some guided completion tasks; its controlled Qwen Magicoder checkpoints show non-monotonic, task-specific changes.

IFIM reports higher instruction-conditioned scores than base models on IHumanEval and IRepoMasterEval for DeepSeek-Coder and Qwen2.5-Coder, usually preserving non-instructed scores. It also evaluates 100 real developer TODO/FIXME instructions mined from commits after the evaluated models' training cutoff.
counterevidence: The Code Talkers paper has family-, size- and benchmark-specific exceptions, and explicitly warns about possible benchmark contamination, undisclosed training data, and lack of real IDE/user evaluation.

IFIM is trained on 122.9k examples whose instruction text was synthesized by GPT-4.1; its two main code families and 100-item developer sample do not establish broad external validity. One Qwen IFIM ordering substantially regresses without instructions.
IFIM truncates repository context to 20 lines at each side and explicitly leaves thousand-token repository contexts to future work.
falsifiable_test: Compare base, generic-instruct and IFIM models from matched backbones on post-cutoff, repository-level FIM tasks with no instruction, accurate instruction, ambiguous instruction and misleading comments. Hold training tokens, compute, prompt format and test budget fixed; report paired correctness, boundary/format violations, runtime/complexity on growing test inputs, developer acceptance, and results by language/context length. The mitigation claim weakens if IFIM's gains vanish on held-out repositories or long contexts, or if non-instruct capability consistently drops; it strengthens if gains replicate across models/languages without correctness or stability regressions.
limitations: Two recent primary studies; IFIM's held-out developer set is only 100 items and its instruction training is synthetic. No independent replication or IDE user study in this batch. The finding is not a claim that a particular tuning method is novel or production-ready.

topic: code generation evaluation; algorithmic complexity; runtime stability
status: bounded full-text finding from one multi-model arXiv preprint
claim: Functional pass@k alone can hide meaningful structural/runtime diversity among outputs that pass public tests. Stability-aware measurements are a plausible complement, but the sampled paper's SCTD/DCTD/BEF metrics remain candidate diagnostics rather than validated predictors of production risk.
positive_evidence: Dynamic Stability evaluates 11 models on BigO(Bench)'s 311-problem test set plus CodeContests and reports structural/runtime trace divergence among solutions passing public tests.
Its temperature study usually reports higher pass@1 accompanied by higher structural and dynamic divergence, illustrating a possible correctness-versus-predictability tradeoff.
The authors give concrete examples where algorithmically distinct correct solutions have different complexity and runtime profiles.
counterevidence: Each model-problem-temperature setting uses five samples, which the authors say may undersample output variance.

Evaluation runs in Python; test-suite coverage and lack of adequate asymptotic cases limit interpretation. BEF can signal structural/runtime mismatch but is not shown to predict production incidents, tail latency or resource cost in live systems.
The observed temperature pattern is not a proof of a universal monotonic relationship across models, decoding settings or coding tasks.

sources.sections: Secs. 2.2-2.4, results/temperature analysis, Threats to Validity

falsifiable_test: On a contamination-resistant multi-language benchmark, draw substantially more than five samples per prompt over a preregistered temperature grid, identify functionally correct solutions, then measure asymptotic scaling, runtime/energy distributions and worst-case/tail behavior on expanding hidden tests. Compare SCTD/DCTD/BEF against these external outcomes. The complementarity claim weakens if these metrics add no predictive information beyond pass@k and static complexity analysis; it strengthens if they predict held-out performance variance and resource tails.
limitations: One recent preprint; small per-condition generation count and author-acknowledged language and test-suite limits. This batch does not reproduce the metrics or validate them on deployed systems.
